row.name: Northwest Slopes
row.overview: Huron's standard trail: forest switchbacks to timberline near 11,800 ft, a big grassy basin, the saddle toward Browns Peak, then the rocky northern crest to the summit.

row.name: East Face
row.overview: Rockfall threatens everyone here; stay quick and watch the rope. A scramble leads from Iceberg Lake to the notch above the First Tower, followed by the Washboard. The Fresh Air Traverse is exposed, with fixed pitons on its left and a belay in a chimney. The Grand Staircase then gives three pitches up to the crux offwidth, with the summit up and right over easy terrain.
row.approach: From the Whitney Portal trailhead, follow the Whitney Trail a short way to the North Fork of Lone Pine Creek, where a climbers' trail leaves it and climbs a wooded slope into a willow-choked valley. Where the valley tightens, a third-class chute in the canyon wall leads onto the Ebersbacher Ledges, which skirt the worst of the brush and end at Lower Boy Scout Lake. Continue past Upper Boy Scout Lake over slabs, talus and moraine, then up a gully through the last band of cliffs to Iceberg Lake, the usual camp for the east side. From the lake, scramble up the east side of the towers to the gap that separates the two lowest towers, where the roped climbing begins. A Whitney Zone permit from Inyo National Forest is required: a day-use permit for a car-to-car push, or an overnight North Fork permit if you camp.
row.descent_text: The climb ends on the summit plateau. Descend the Mountaineers Route: from the summit, walk west across the plateau to where the route topped out, and note the spot, since the rim all looks alike from above. Steep, exposed third-class steps and ledges lead to the notch, then a long loose gully runs east to Iceberg Lake; some fourth-class downclimbing is possible near the top. Early in the season, or after storms, snow and ice can stay in the upper gully into summer, so carry an axe and crampons, wear a helmet against rockfall, and do not glissade the upper gully, where hidden ice can send you out of control. Parties have rappelled the icy upper section on slings left on the left side of the gully.
row.best_season: Guided ascents run from late June through October, when the summer high-altitude window is open.

row.name: U-Notch Couloir
row.overview: A broad ice gully rising from the glacier into the wide gap beside the summit. Getting over the bergschrund is the main difficulty. Beyond the gap, a pair of pitches on easy-going cracks reach the summit area. Parties usually take the Clyde variation rather than the chimney variation.

row.name: Swiss Arete
row.overview: Granite cracks carry about 6 moderate pitches on steep steps. The rock beats the Matterhorn namesake's, in a remoter setting. Sam Mack Meadow is the approach point; the Glacier Notch couloir and then the L-Shaped Couloir lead to the ridge. P4 holds the crux, an impasse that forces a sideways step right across a slab with exposure; a further two pitches reach the summit.

row.name: East Arete
row.approach: From the Whitney Portal trailhead, follow the Whitney Trail a short way to the North Fork of Lone Pine Creek, where a climbers' trail leaves it, then use the Ebersbacher Ledges past Lower Boy Scout Lake to Upper Boy Scout Lake, the usual camp for this route. Climb the scree north of the lake up to the Russell-Carillon saddle, then head west up the ridge, keeping right where needed, to the east summit. The summit ridge is crossed mostly on its right side to the west summit. A permit is required: an overnight North Fork permit if you camp, or a Whitney Zone day-use permit.
row.descent_text: Descend the way you climbed: back along the East Ridge, with exposed but solid third class near the summits, to the Russell-Carillon pass, then easy scree down to Upper Boy Scout Lake. From the west summit you can alternatively use the South Gully, via a third-class ramp just before the east summit, if camped at Iceberg Lake; it is loose but quick.

row.name: Northeast Couloir
row.overview: The big gully that separates Split Mountain from its aretes. It funnels rockfall from many gullies, so approach with caution. The bergschrund can be large, and pitch 1 beyond it is an ice smear, vertical in places, over a bulge. Options then include an ice chimney on the left, the center flow (thin and mixed when poor), or two moderate chossy rock pitches. Next, cross over to the primary flow, which gives up to 600 feet of low-angle ice. A snowfield above ranges from deep facets to hard neve. Rockfall danger is extreme in the late-season upper pitches. From the top turn right on class 3 to the summit.
row.approach: From the Red Lakes trailhead, the trail starts a little north of Red Mountain Creek and switchbacks uphill, then turns west and runs above the creek to Red Lake and the foot of Split Mountain. The couloir starts a long way up the slope above Red Lake. The couloir is a funnel for rockfall.

row.name: Northeast Arete
row.overview: NE corner route to the summit, which lies southeast along the ridge. Sound rock gives a scramble of 3rd plus 4th class, then a ledge belay 150 feet up. Mid-route has somewhat loose rock where the line bears left at the fork of the Y. Climbers left near the edge has the best exposure. The final 100 feet steepen, with mid 5th directly or easier ground right.

row.name: From Trail by W + N ridge
row.overview: Be ready to down-climb: no rappel anchors are known near the top. Two 5.6 moves, an overhang and a narrow gap, are hard to reverse. Beforehand come sculpted granite (about 5.4), talus and a weakness in a short wall; afterward a slab traverse southward to the Normal route and then a wide crack to the crest.
